sources.note: Nothing on Terebu. Terebu appears only as a row in the Proto Schouten consonant/vowel correspondence tables and in cognate sets (data source 'Kaiep (Terebu) Laycock n.d.', App. B); p. 123: 'Kaiep and Terebu (related at dialect level)'. sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm D. 1985. Current use and expansion of Tok Pisin: effects of Tok Pisin on some vernacular languages. In S. A. Wurm & P. Mühlhäusler (eds), Handbook of Tok Pisin (New Guinea Pidgin), 539-556. Pacific Linguistics C-70. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-C70.539.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone; the paper is about grammatical and lexical transference from Tok Pisin and says explicitly (p. 539) 'we have no cases of phonological transferences'. Kaiep content: glossed sentences showing Tok Pisin pinis (completive), bai (future), save/mas/laik (modals), tu, na, sapos, long/wantaim/bilong (prepositions) in Kaiep, with remarks that Kaiep, like Kairiru, lacked native prepositions. Terebu content: pp. 549-550 'two pieces of evidence indicate that Kaiep also lacked a native category of preposition. Firstly, Laycock's (1971) fieldnotes from Terebu, a dialect of Kaiep…

sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Nothing. Survey and classification with comparative wordlist; Terebu named once (Kaiep speakers 'scattered throughout Terebu and Samap villages'); the phonological remarks (p. 404) concern stop voicing, palatalisation and loss of POC *k, no stress for any Sepik Austronesian language.

sources.citation: Laycock, D. C. 1976. History of research in Austronesian languages: Sepik Provinces. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 73-93. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: No phonology content. It is a research history: p. 80 'East of Wewak, on the coast, the next AN language is that of Kaiep, for which there are no published linguistic data, and considerable confusion in naming.. Terebu is now divided between Kaiep and Bungain (NAN) speakers'; p. 80-81: Capell elicited his own wordlist from 'Turupu' but it was the Bungain language; Laycock's own 1970-71 materials cover Kaiep (brief wordlists and grammatical materials), Kairiru and Kaiep 'very closely related'. Establishes that up to 1976 no description (missionary or academic) of Kaiep/Terebu existed.
